newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crudes plummet on Iraq renewal prospects.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crudes plummet on Iraq renewal prospects.

text.p: U.S. cash crude oil markets Tuesday reacted negatively to confirmation the United States will support renewal of the $2 billion U.N./Iraq oil-for-food accord, effectively ensuring Security Council approval.
Outright cash July West Texas Intermediate/Cushing talked late in the session some 50 cents weaker at $20.40-50 a barrel, tracking losses on the NYMEX futures markets.
July futures lost 65 cents to settle at $20.33, but cash benchmark benefits from a 15 cents premium to the screen due to strong July Exchange for Physical (EFP) markets.
"July/August spreads were last talked at minus 4-8 cents, considering the EFPs at plus 15 cents," said a cash trader.
Traders said technical selling worked hand-in-hand with the U.N./Iraq developments, deflating futures prices from the opening bell.
Even though most indications pointed to the U.S. approving another six months of Iraq oil sales, traders said market sentiment allowed increased selling on the news.
Confirmation came when U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns announced mid-afternoon that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had decided in favor of extending the deal.
In recent weeks, the U.S. had refused to acknowledge its intentions on the matter, leaving markets to speculate on possible objections from Washington.
But now, all hurdles seem clear for renewal of the accord at the present $2 billion oil sales cap for another 180 days.
The Security Council was to discuss the issue on Wednesday, considering a comprehensive report by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan recommending approval.
A renewal vote could come Wednesday, or as late as Friday ahead of the deal's expiration on Saturday, June 7.
U.S. domestic grade differentials tracked a mostly steady path against declining WTI/Cushing outrights.

Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James sold last at a 15 cents discount to the marker, steady from Monday. Traders said the push-pull in the LLS market saw differentials balanced at 16-12 cents under July WTI/Cushing.
On the one hand, LLS benefits from the narrowing Brent-WTI arbitrage, preventing North Sea Brent deliveries to the Gulf.
On the bearish side, LLS was pressured by softer Dated Brent values, and slack refiner demand, traders said.
Last deals confirmed for West Texas Sour/Midland were steady at WTI/Cushing -$1.55, with Eugene Island steady at $1.65-55 under benchmark.
Dealers were also recorded for July Postings at $1.92 and $1.95, and for Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire at benchmark minus 64 cents.

Traders said EFP premiums remained firm despite some chatter that mid-continent refiners were looking for sweet barrels, opening some opportunity to unload unwanted foreign supplies delivered against NYMEX in May and June.
American Petroleum Instiute (API) data showed crude stocks 8.8 million barrels higher for week-ended May 23, gasoline levels 2.95 million barrels higher and distillates 5.09 million barrels heavier.
Utilization rates also increased from 96.7 percent to 98.4 percent.
Prior to the report's release, a Reuters survey on trader expectations saw crude building a slight 313,000 barrels, distillates adding 2 million barrels and gasoline drawing 500,000 barrels.
ACCESS trading saw outrights decrease around 10-15 cents for July WTI/Cushing immediately after the API release.
--Patrick Connole, NY Energy Desk, ((+1 212 859 1828))
